Photograph: Teton county search and rescue View image in fullscreen William Standish lost contact with his family as he was hiking in Wyoming. Photograph: Teton county search and rescue Wyoming Missing Australian hiker found dead in Wyoming, officials say Body of William Standish discovered in Teton mountains as investigators say fatal fall likely cause of death Edward Helmore Fri 31 Jul 2026 17.06 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 17.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 28-year-old Australian hiker who lost contact with his family while hiking the Continental Divide Trail between Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks in Wyoming has been found dead, according to authorities. The man, identified as William Standish, was discovered by rescuers on Wednesday morning in the Wigwams, a series of rocky peaks on the west slope of the Teton mountain range, the Teton county coroner said. Investigators say it was likely he suffered a fatal fall. Standish had been attempting a thru-hike of the Continental Divide Trail between the Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks when he disappeared after contacting his family on 23 July, according to a statement from Teton county rescuers. Evidence suggests Standish may have fallen from a steep ridgeline that separates Grand Teton and the Jedediah Smith wilderness, officials said. Standish was discovered by a helicopter team after it spotted an orange backpack – and then saw his remains below the ridge. His family said it had stopped receiving updates from him via a Garmin GPS device and Facebook Messenger on 23 July, leading to a search being mounted by Teton county rescue crews. On 19 July, Standish gave an update from a location near Old Faithful, and described his planned route in the Tetons, Gros Ventre wilderness, the Wind River range, and the Divide Basin. Four days later, the family received a Garmin check-in without coordinates or a message. There was also a Facebook Messenger video that they believe placed him in the Wigwams. The Teton county search and rescue team said it “sends its sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased”. It also expressed gratitude to federal agencies who assisted in searching for Standish. Standish had reportedly been following a popular thru-hike, or end-to-end through-hike, starting in Canada, the most northern point of the 3,100-mile Continental Divide Trail – which passes down through Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and New Mexico. There have been other hiking-related deaths in North America recently. The Colorado Sun reported that a 15-year-old boy died after being struck by lightning on the state’s Mount Blue Sky on Monday. Sheriff’s officials identified the boy as Levi Strobel. Four other people were seriously injured, including Levi’s younger brother. In Arizona, a man died during a hike on Phoenix’s South Mountain. Richard Fletcher, 61, left his home early on Saturday morning. Investigators later said his death was consistent with a heat-related or medical event, authorities told local media . A 62-year-old man died in New Hampshire when he suffered a medical emergency in the state’s Welch-Dickey trail in the White Mountains. He was evacuated by national guard helicopter and later pronounced dead, according to New Hampshire Public Radio . Two hikers also died in Canada’s Banff national park. One was a woman in her 20s after falling from a mountain near Marvel Peak on Tuesday. Three days earlier, a 65-year-old from Calgary fell from Mount Temple, also in Banff, the CBC reported. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Pro-Palestinian march in London Israel-Gaza war Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’ March is first since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful Sammy Gecsoyler Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.52 EDT Last modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 12.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel . The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza. Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025. Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media. “Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger and not going anywhere. Thank you all,” he said. By Saturday afternoon, organisers said 250,000 people were at the march. ‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins Read more The Metropolitan police have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to “minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities”. The Metropolitan police posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place. “Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action. “We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.” The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. At Labour party conference last month, Miliband appeared to reference the marches , which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.” Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: “We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.” Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be “significant”. “We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,” Galvin continued. The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm. British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband Read more A counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags. The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration “to minimise the risk of serious disruption”. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm. Last Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in central London was held. The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to “exercise [their] right to protest on a different date” and admitted that finding the organisers had been “frankly difficult”. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march. The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain. Research has found 94% of homes destroyed in the black summer fires were within the 100m buffer zone to identify at-risk properties. Photograph: Christine Tondorf/The Guardian View image in fullscreen House on the NSW north coast destroyed by bushfire in 2019. Research has found 94% of homes destroyed in the black summer fires were within the 100m buffer zone to identify at-risk properties. Photograph: Christine Tondorf/The Guardian Bushfires Almost all NSW homes destroyed in black summer bushfires were within 100 metres of flammable vegetation Exclusive : Research confirms official advice about high-risk properties and warns worsening conditions will make more homes unsafe Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here Graham Readfearn Climate and environment correspondent Sat 17 Oct 2026 15.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 15.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Almost every home destroyed in New South Wales during the black summer bushfires of 2019 and 2020 was inside the 100 metre buffer zone used to identify properties most at risk, new research has found. The findings are an endorsement of the risk maps used by authorities, but the research warns that as global heating generates ever-worsening fire conditions firefighters may have to extend the recommended distances between homes and vegetation to keep homes safe. The NSW rural fire service said the findings reinforced how homes in high risk areas should be built to higher fire standards as it prepared for a potentially “challenging” fire season. More than 3,000 homes were lost across the country during the unprecedented fires six years ago that took 33 lives and killed or displaced almost 3 billion native animals. Of the 2,475 homes lost in NSW, the research, published in the International Journal of Wildland Fire , found 94% were less than 100 metres away from flammable vegetation such as trees. The 100 metre buffer is a key part of the widely used maps of bushfire prone land that firefighters use to plan local outreach activities, and planning authorities use to assess how bushfire-resistant new homes and renovations should be. ‘Catastrophic wildfire loop’ after colonisation left parts of Australia more at risk from bushfires, study finds Read more Associate professor Owen Price, an expert in bushfire risk at the University of Wollongong who led the research, said the findings showed a key aspect of the method to identify buildings at risk from bushfires was “more or less spot on”. “That’s reassuring. Distance to vegetation is really important and that 100 metre rule that they apply is pretty good,” he said. But the research also examined fire danger ratings – an index that combines temperature, wind, humidity and the dryness of fuel – on the days when each home was lost. When the fire danger ratings – known technically as the Forest Fire Danger Index – reached extreme or catastrophic conditions, “houses further away [than 100 metres] were burning,” said Price. “That’s a warning sign, because we know that index is going to get worse [from global heating]. We know the direction of travel.” Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter He said wildfire researchers were alarmed by the increasing number of fires around the world hitting and moving through urban areas, including the 2025 Los Angeles Eaton fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged thousands of homes and businesses. Part of his own research was aimed at understanding if similar events could be replicated in Australia. “Being very close to another house [that is on fire] is another risk factor, which is why it’s important we stop houses from burning,” he said. The research warned that the “current regulation may become less useful over time” as the climate crisis increased the risk of homes being lost. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When he publishes Sign up to Clear Air Australia Adam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisis after newsletter promotion Melissa O’Halloran, responsible for work on bushfire planning at the NSW rural fire service, said the research showed that “houses in that [bushfire prone] area should be built to a higher construction standard”. “The conditions in 2019 were extreme and outside what we would usually prepare for and, even under those conditions, our policy has stood up pretty well. “This reinforces why we want people to have bushfire protection measures in place.” O’Halloran said investigations carried out after previous fires had shown that not all residents knew they were actually living in a bushfire prone area. Homes within bushfire prone land in the state are allowed to remove trees within 10 metres of a house and clear understory within 50 metres . She said the service was reviewing its main bushfire protection policy that would consider the increasing climate risk. “We’re seeing the impacts of climate change already. It isn’t just temperatures, it’s also about how quickly the landscape dries out, as well as extreme pyroconvective fires,” she said. Inspector James Morris, of the NSW rural fire service, said there was already heightened risk this year for fires in northern parts of the state, in the central west and the far south coast. “They’ve had high rainfall, and it does not take long for those fuels to dry out. It is important residents do their bit and prepare,” he said. “We could be in for a challenging fire season.” Explore more on these topics Bushfires Natural disasters New South Wales Wildfires Climate crisis news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
